content: HIV testing is being offered to students aged 12 years and older in schools. However, school-based HIV testing programs remain controversial, and only a few countries have implemented such initiatives. Further evaluation is necessary to address issues related to confidentiality, linkage to care, and adolescents' experiences and expectations regarding school-based testing for both viral hepatitis and HIV. Additionally, the impact and acceptability of testing among university students need to be assessed. Testing in prisons and other correctional facilities is a potentially effective strategy to increase testing uptake among high-risk populations, as many prisoners are at an elevated risk of acquiring hepatitis B and C infections. However, implementing testing programs in prison settings involves additional ethical and regulatory considerations. For example, in Victoria, Australia, the prevalence of hepatitis C among prisoners is high at 25%, and new transmissions also occur within prisons. A state-wide program was initiated to eliminate viral hepatitis transmission in its 13 prisons through the assessment, education, and management of prisoners with chronic viral hepatitis. All prisoners are screened for viral hepatitis upon entry or transfer, and those who test positive are referred to the Victorian State-wide Prison Hepatitis Program for further assessment and antiviral therapy. This therapy is supervised by trained clinical nurse consultants during visits every 2–4 weeks. The program is integrated into the prison primary care system and utilizes telemedicine for consultations with part-time hepatologists, with direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) provided since March 2015. Effective health system programming practices for viral hepatitis testing, care, and treatment can be informed by the global scale-up of HIV testing and treatment. Delivery models, such as workplace, school, and community-based settings, as well as task-shifting responsibilities to trained lay providers, were originally developed to improve HIV testing delivery. Incorporating these practices may enhance the accessibility of hepatitis testing and linkage to care in certain settings. Simplified diagnostic tests and treatment regimens for viral hepatitis allow for decentralization and task-shifting in service delivery models, particularly in areas with limited access to hospital facilities and laboratory services. Integration of viral hepatitis testing with other health services involves not only providing related services in a single setting but also linking recording and reporting systems to share information and referrals between settings and providers. This includes clinical services for tuberculosis (TB), HIV, maternal and child health, sexual and reproductive health, mental health, harm reduction programs for people who inject drugs (PWID), migrant and refugee services, and prison populations. Integration with HIV testing and treatment services is particularly relevant in settings with high HBV and HCV prevalence and coexisting high HIV prevalence. The primary purpose of integration is to make HBV, HCV, and HIV testing more convenient for individuals accessing health facilities for other reasons, thereby expanding the reach and uptake of viral hepatitis testing. For patients, integration may address multiple health needs simultaneously, saving time and money. For health systems, integration can reduce service duplication, improve coordination, and enhance overall efficiency and cost-effectiveness. Decentralization of hepatitis testing services involves delivering services in peripheral health facilities, community-based venues, and locations closer to patients' homes, rather than relying solely on urban hospital sites. This approach can reduce transportation costs and waiting times, improving testing uptake. Decentralization has been a key component of the global scale-up of HIV services in high-burden lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), successfully increasing testing uptake and reducing loss to follow-up. With the development of simpler diagnostic tests and treatment regimens for HBV and HCV, decentralization has the potential to increase hepatitis testing uptake. However, decentralization may not always be appropriate or acceptable to potential users. In some settings, centralized services may provide greater anonymity for high-risk populations or those fearing stigma and discrimination. Additionally, in low-prevalence settings, decentralizing hepatitis testing may be inefficient and costly. Decisions about decentralization should consider context, needs, access to laboratory infrastructure, and overall costs and benefits. Task-shifting or task-sharing in the delivery of hepatitis testing is a pragmatic response to health workforce shortages. It aims to increase the effectiveness and efficiency of available personnel, enabling the existing workforce to provide testing services to more people. Systematic reviews from various healthcare areas support the conclusion that good health outcomes can be achieved by delegating tasks to nurses and lay or community health workers, provided they receive appropriate training and supervision. Task-shifting has been adopted for over a decade to expand HIV testing in resource-limited settings across the Americas, Europe, sub-Saharan Africa, and Asia. The World Health Organization (WHO) now recommends that trained and supervised lay providers can independently perform HIV counseling and testing using rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs). Incorporating viral hepatitis testing into existing task-shifting models for HIV services could be an effective and cost-efficient means of achieving testing and treatment objectives. Peer-led interventions have also been effective in increasing viral hepatitis testing, care, and treatment for marginalized groups of PWID. Peers can act as role models and provide non-judgmental and respectful support, reducing stigma, facilitating access to services, and improving their acceptability. However, increasing task-shifting and broadening the scope of responsibilities for trained lay providers alone will not fully address staff shortages and poor-quality services. Diagnostic innovations have created new opportunities for enhancing hepatitis testing and monitoring treatment response. Simplified single virological assay testing algorithms, near-patient or point-of-care (POC) assays for nucleic acid testing (NAT) and core antigen, dried blood spot (DBS) sampling, multiplex platforms, and self-testing are among the future directions in testing. Simplifying testing algorithms is critical for affordability and scaling up testing. Near-patient or POC testing technologies, such as molecular NAT-based tests, are crucial for expanding hepatitis testing services, especially in community-based settings. These devices are easier to use, require minimal training, and provide results within two hours. Multiplex RDTs, which can detect multiple pathogens simultaneously, are in development and may improve client flow and reduce patient visits and transportation costs. Self-testing, where individuals collect a specimen, perform a test, and interpret the result themselves, is a promising approach to expand access to testing in the future. Hepatitis testing must emphasize the WHO's five Cs (consent, confidentiality, counseling, correct results, and connection to care). Testing should never be mandatory, compulsory, or coercive. All testing sites should have standard operating procedures (SOPs) and ethical codes of conduct to protect client information and confidentiality. Testing should follow WHO strategies and validated national algorithms, with appropriate quality assurance mechanisms in place. Testing should be part of a care pathway that includes access to prevention, treatment, and vaccination services. Priority for testing should focus on diagnosing the undiagnosed, identifying those in greatest need of treatment, and those at the highest risk of transmitting infection.
